quests.question: ___ is my favorite hobby.
quests.hint: This word acts as the subject of the sentence, like a noun.
quests.explanation: A gerund (-ing form) can act as the subject of a sentence, functioning like a noun: Swimming is my favorite hobby. 'Swim' alone can't be a subject on its own.

quests.question: She's interested in ___ a new language.
quests.hint: Verbs after a preposition like 'in' take a special form.
quests.explanation: Verbs following a preposition always take the gerund form: interested in learning. 'To learn' cannot follow a preposition this way.

quests.question:
— What do you do for fun?
— I'm really into ___ photos.
quests.hint: 'Into' works like a preposition here too.
quests.explanation: 'Into' functions as a preposition, so the following verb takes the gerund form: into taking photos, following the same rule from Question 2.

quests.question: I enjoy ___ books in my free time.
quests.hint: This verb always takes the -ing form after it.
quests.explanation: 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund: enjoy reading. This is a fixed pattern that simply needs to be memorized.

quests.question: She finished ___ her homework before dinner.
quests.hint: This verb, like 'enjoy', always takes the -ing form.
quests.explanation: 'Finish' always takes a gerund: finished doing. Verbs like 'enjoy' and 'finish' are part of a group that never uses the infinitive form after them.

quests.question:
— Do you want to go out?
— I'd rather avoid ___ in this weather.
quests.hint: This verb also belongs to the gerund-only group.
quests.explanation: 'Avoid' always takes a gerund: avoid going. Like 'enjoy' and 'finish', it never pairs with 'to' + verb.

quests.question: I want ___ a new car next year.
quests.hint: This verb always takes 'to' + base verb after it.
quests.explanation: 'Want' is always followed by an infinitive: want to buy. This is the opposite pattern from verbs like 'enjoy', which take a gerund instead.

quests.question: She decided ___ her job.
quests.hint: This verb, like 'want', always takes an infinitive.
quests.explanation: 'Decide' always takes an infinitive: decided to quit. It belongs to the same group of verbs as 'want', 'hope', and 'plan'.

quests.question:
— What are your plans?
— I plan ___ abroad next summer.
quests.hint: This verb also belongs to the infinitive-only group.
quests.explanation: 'Plan' always takes an infinitive: plan to travel, following the same pattern practiced with 'want' and 'decide'.

quests.question: I stopped ___ coffee; it was keeping me awake at night.
quests.hint: This means ending an ongoing habit completely.
quests.explanation: 'Stop + gerund' means ending an ongoing habit or activity: stopped drinking coffee (no longer drinks it at all).

quests.question: I stopped ___ a coffee on my way to work.
quests.hint: This means pausing one activity in order to do something else.
quests.explanation: 'Stop + infinitive' means pausing to do something else: stopped to drink coffee (paused walking in order to drink). This is a completely different meaning from Question 1.

quests.question:
— Did you remember to call her?
— Yes, I remember ___ her yesterday.
quests.hint: This describes remembering a completed past action, not a future duty.
quests.explanation: 'Remember + gerund' describes recalling something already done: remember calling her (recalls the memory of the call itself), unlike 'remember + infinitive', which would describe not forgetting a future task.

quests.question: I had my hair ___ yesterday.
quests.hint: This causative structure needs the past participle, since someone else did the action.
quests.explanation: Causative 'have something done' uses the past participle: had my hair cut, meaning someone else cut it, not the speaker.

quests.question: She's getting her car ___ tomorrow.
quests.hint: This uses the same causative pattern, with 'get' instead of 'have'.
quests.explanation: 'Get something done' follows the same pattern as 'have something done': getting her car repaired, meaning a mechanic will do it.

quests.question:
— Did you paint the house yourself?
— No, I had it ___ by professionals.
quests.hint: Someone else did the painting, matching the causative pattern.
quests.explanation: 'Had it painted' shows someone else did the work, following the same causative pattern practiced in Questions 1 and 2.

quests.question: She said, 'I am tired.' → She said that she ___ tired.
quests.hint: In reported speech, present tense usually shifts one step back into the past.
quests.explanation: Reported speech typically backshifts present to past: 'am' becomes 'was'. The original words change to reflect that time has passed since they were spoken.

quests.question: He said, 'I will call you.' → He said that he ___ call me.
quests.hint: 'Will' also shifts back one step in reported speech.
quests.explanation: 'Will' backshifts to 'would' in reported speech: said he would call, following the same backshifting pattern as Question 1.

quests.question:
— What did she say?
— She said she ___ finished the project already.
quests.hint: Present perfect also shifts back a step in reported speech.
quests.explanation: Present perfect ('has finished') backshifts to past perfect ('had finished') in reported speech, continuing the same time-shift pattern from this level.
quests.grammarRule: Reported Speech: Present Perfect to Past Perfect

quests.question: 'Where do you live?' → She asked me ___ I lived.
quests.hint: This keeps the same question word from the original question.
quests.explanation: Reported WH-questions keep the original question word: asked where I lived. Notice the word order also changes to statement order (I lived), not question order.

quests.question: 'Are you coming?' → He asked if I ___ coming.
quests.hint: This yes/no question uses 'if', and the verb needs to backshift into the past.
quests.explanation: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' (or 'whether'), and 'are' backshifts to 'was': asked if I was coming.

quests.question:
— What did he ask?
— He asked me what time it ___ .
quests.hint: This is another WH-question needing the past tense shift.
quests.explanation: 'Is' backshifts to 'was' in this reported WH-question: asked what time it was, keeping statement word order.

quests.question: 'Close the door,' she said. → She told me ___ the door.
quests.hint: Reported commands use 'told someone' followed by this special verb form.
quests.explanation: Reported commands follow the pattern 'told someone + infinitive': told me to close the door, turning the direct command into reported speech.

quests.question: 'Please help me,' he said. → He asked me ___ him.
quests.hint: Reported requests follow the same pattern as reported commands, just with 'asked' instead of 'told'.
quests.explanation: Reported requests use 'asked someone + infinitive', just like commands: asked me to help, following the same pattern from Question 1.

quests.question:
— What did the teacher say?
— She told us ___ quiet during the test.
quests.hint: This is another reported command, following the same fixed pattern.
quests.explanation: 'Told us to be quiet' follows the same reported command pattern practiced throughout this level: told + person + infinitive.

quests.question: I enjoy ___ new places when I travel.
quests.hint: This verb always takes the gerund form, reviewed from Level 152.
quests.explanation: 'Enjoy' always takes a gerund: enjoy visiting, reviewing the pattern from Level 152.

quests.question: She wants ___ her own business someday.
quests.hint: This verb always takes the infinitive form, reviewed from Level 153.
quests.explanation: 'Want' always takes an infinitive: wants to start, reviewing the pattern from Level 153.

quests.question:
— What did he tell you?
— He told me ___ careful on the road.
quests.hint: This is the same reported command structure from Level 158.
quests.explanation: 'Told me to be careful' follows the reported command pattern practiced in Level 158: told + person + infinitive.

quests.question: All employees are required ___ the new safety training by Friday.
quests.hint: 'Required' pairs with the infinitive form, a common structure in workplace memos.
quests.explanation: 'Required to' takes the infinitive: required to complete, a very common structure in official workplace communication.

quests.question: The manager suggested ___ the meeting to next week.
quests.hint: This verb always takes the gerund form, like 'enjoy' and 'avoid'.
quests.explanation: 'Suggest' always takes a gerund: suggested moving, joining the same group as 'enjoy', 'finish', and 'avoid' from earlier in this stage.

quests.question:
— What did she say about the deadline?
— She said the deadline ___ been extended.
quests.hint: This closes Stage 8 with the same present-perfect-to-past-perfect shift from Level 156.
quests.explanation: 'Has been extended' backshifts to 'had been extended' in reported speech, closing out the full journey through gerunds, infinitives, causatives, and reported speech covered across Levels 151 to 160.
quests.grammarRule: Reported Speech: Present Perfect to Past Perfect
